#650. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies

To explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies."

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research

The results raise important questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?"

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support."

The researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

#649. Record Store Day Co-Founder on How Black Friday Evolved Into a Major Holiday for Vinyl Hounds, and What Will Fly Off the Shelves This Year

The biggest shopping day of the year isn't just for big-box stores. Michael Kurtz predicts which artists, from Noah Kahan to the Beatles, will have LP enthusiasts up and in the shops early

In April of this year, the 19th installment of Record Store Day was the event’s most successful ever, but Nov. 27 brings another opportunity for music junkies to get their vinyl on: Record Store Day Black Friday.

While the O.G. Record Store Day was conceived as a general celebration of independent record stores, and features limited-edition, in-store only releases, the Black Friday edition exists for a different reason: to give those indie stores a slice of the “biggest shopping day of the year” pie. That’s also why the vinyl releases you’ll find making their debuts on Black Friday are more likely to remain there for the rest of the holiday season, and why many stores will make them available on their websites starting on Saturday the 28th.

The concept of hyping local independent record stores as a must for holiday shopping may sound rather obvious, but RSD co-founder Michael Kurtz says that, at first, he was opposed to the idea, which his wife came up with.

“I was not on board with it,” he admits. “My initial response at the time was, ‘Ah, that’s for big-box stores and selling cheap toasters and stuff.’” But eventually, he came around, thinking they could do “a little bit smaller version” for the holidays. RSD Black Friday does feature fewer releases overall, but its main goal is to get customers through the door. “Most record stores do about two months’ worth of business” that day, Kurtz says.

For Black Friday, Kurtz says what you’ll find in the racks is largely thanks to what he calls a “Secret Squirrel group” of about 20 record store owners nationwide, who help winnow down the overwhelming numbers of releases pitched by artists and record labels.

“They’ve been around forever; they run iconic record stores,” Kurtz explains of this crate-digging cabal. “And I go to them and say, ‘Hey, do you think record stores would want to have this?’ Because Black Friday is not the same as Record Store Day. It’s not supposed to be just a limited thing only. It’s also supposed to be things that record stores want to have in their bins year-round.”

But what’s true for both events is that they feature releases from a dizzying array of artists across multiple genres. That big tent approach, Kurtz reveals, was inspired by Metallica bassist Robert Trujillo, who early on convinced Kurtz to do a vinyl release by iconic jazz bassist Jaco Pastorius.

“It went to No. 1 on Billboard‘s jazz chart,” Kurtz recalls. “And that made us rethink: ‘Oh, geez, we could do jazz records, we could do bluegrass records, we could do soul records, R&B, funk.”

Of course, rock in its various forms is still a huge focus of both Record Store Day and RSD Black Friday, but in recent years, pop artists have climbed on board the vinyl train en masse, resulting in a surprising boom in customers who are too young to even remember a world where vinyl was once the only option.

Kurtz says, “The majority of people who come to Record Store Day now and participate are younger than the age of 35, and slightly more female than male.” Of course, you can credit the biggest pop star in the world for that.

While Kurtz says Billie Eilish’s 7-inch releases for RSD “sort of cracked the door open” for that demographic, he notes, “It got blown wide open with Taylor Swift. When she did her ‘Long Pond Studio Sessions’ record with us exclusively for record stores [in 2023], it changed everything.” That album became the first Record Store Day exclusive release ever to hit the top 10 of theBillboard200, proving that brand-new releases on vinyl could do just as well as streaming titles.

For RSD Black Friday 2026, Kurtz predicts that it’ll be Noah Kahan’s vinyls getting the youth through the door. “He’s got a special 7-inch that was done just for record stores that’s very very cool: It’s tied in with the ‘Hunger Games’ soundtrack,” says Kurtz, referring to “Draw You Out,” Kahan’s contribution to “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping – The Album.” “And then he’s also got an additional record that’ll be highly sought after.” That would be “The Last of the Bugs,” which collects the four tracks Kahan added to the expanded edition of his album”The Great Divide.”

Kurtz is also excited about a Bruce Springsteen live box set, the American version of The Beatles’ Rubber Soul LP on gold vinyl, a live album by Billy Joel, a disc of the Doors’ studio sessions and a 2-LP set by Ween “for all the pot smokers out there.”

He also predicts the Miles Davis, Jerry Garcia Band and Grateful Dead releases will be popular, as well as the original, previously unreleased version of Joan Jett’s “I Love Rock & Roll” album and not one but three albums by Japanese guitar virtuoso Masayoshi Takanaka.

Kurtz says he doesn’t even mind that many of those younger customers are buying vinyl not to play, but to display.

“Y’know, I was originally freaked out about that because I’m a music person, but I kind of get it,” he tells me. “Like, I will get the Beatles’ ‘Rubber Soul’ reissue this year and I probably will never open it. I just want it because it’s so beautiful, and to know that I have one of 15,000 copies that will ever be printed … I want to keep it pristine.”

Despite admitting to being “completely anxiety-ridden” each year over how successful each Record Store Day event will be, Kurtz is looking forward to the event’s 20th anniversary next year. He and co-founder Carrie Colliton would love to mark the milestone with live performances and some kind of art installation featuring past Record Store Day releases. (A copy of each of those limited releases is currently stored in a warehouse in Raleigh, North Carolina, in case you might want to pull off the vinyl equivalent of robbing Fort Knox.) But for right now, Kurtz notes, those plans are “dreams right now. They’re not reality.”

Still, the failure he fears is unlikely. Nearly 20 years into an event which has helped drive pop culture back to the vinyl age, Kurtz says there’s no sign of its popularity tapering off. As he notes, “demand for [vinyl] and the excitement around it is completely still there – even more so, I think.” But, he acknowledges, “The only thing that’s a bit alarming is how expensive it’s becoming” – a reflection of the rising cost of shipping due to increases in gas and diesel.

“It’s stunning for me as a person who’s ridden this tiger called Record Store Day for almost 20 years to see it from the beginning: When we first started we were the only ones doing new vinyl, and in the used bins you could find [high quality copies of] Led Zeppelin or the Beatles or Pink Floyd for $3, $5 — those days are over.” Related Stories 'Ramayana' VFX House DNEG Partners With Meta on 3D Movies for VR Glasses, Including 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' (EXCLUSIVE) Meta Launches 150-Plus 3D Movies to Rent and Buy on Quest VR Headsets, With Thousands More Coming in 2027

Kurtz says it was interesting working with shops in the early days, and still can be today — because they’re independent in all sorts of ways, including what they prefer to emphasize in their stores and sometimes think RSD should focus on as a whole.

“The most difficult thing about putting it together was working with record store owners, because they’re a very creative bunch,” he says. “They’re very different; they’re not people who typically play by the rules. They like to do things their way. So to try to get them all together to do this was very difficult.” He adds, “I was in London once and there was a record store owner who just just raked me over the coals because we’d done the Taylor Swift record. I was like, ‘What records do you like?’ He’s like, ‘Yes, Black Sabbath, Deep Purple …’ and I said, ‘OK I get it. That’s what you love and what you’re passionate about, but there’s another generation.’ And so it’s working with them and not alienating them, because sometimes I do that by accident.”

#648. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."

Materials provided by University of Mississippi. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#647. BBC’s Antisemitism Crisis Represents an Unprecedented Chapter for the World’s Most Trusted News Organization

On Thursday, government adviser Lord John Mann announced he is launching an investigation into alleged antisemitism at the broadcaster. It is an unprecedented chapter for the corporation, long held up as one of the most venerable and reliable media institutions in the world.

For those who have been paying attention, however, the move is not surprising following a litany of public missteps dating as far back as 2021, when BBC News misreported an incident in which a group of Jewish students were attacked on a bus in Central London and then doubled down on it, despite eventually acknowledging the reporting lacked accuracy and impartiality. Related Stories Documentaries at the Oscars: A History of Breaking Out of Their Category — and What It Means for ‘You Can See Everything’ Governors Awards 2026: Glenn Close, Ridley Scott and More Receive Honorary Oscars From The Academy (Live Updates)

Later, the broadcaster steadfastly refused to reprimand Gary Lineker, one of its most high-profile sports anchors, as he repeatedly breached its much-touted social media guidelines, which were instituted precisely because of Lineker’s increasingly political Twitter activity. Under the guidelines, high-profile presenters hosting flagship programs are expected to be impartial while the show is on air and for a two-week window before and after. At the time, he called the guidelines “very sensible.”

It was only when last year Lineker reposted an Instagram story about “Zionists” alongside a rat emoji that the BBC finally cut him loose. Even then, rather than a punitive measure, his exit was presented to the public as a mutually agreed decision for the host to leave after the final “Match of the Day” episode aired the following week. The BBC’s press release went on to call him a “defining voice in football coverage” and “thank him for the contribution he has made.”

Critics compared the BBC’s apparently favorable treatment of Lineker to that of former BBC Radio 5 Live broadcaster Danny Baker, who was sacked immediately in 2019 after tweeting an image of a chimpanzee with the caption “Royal baby leaves hospital” just days after Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, gave birth, with the BBC calling it a “serious error of judgment.”

The following month saw yet another incident when the BBC broadcast a little-known rapper’s rant about a former (apparently Jewish) boss, described alternately as a “fucking Zionist” and “bald-headed cunt,” before the crowd was engaged in a chant of “Death to the IDF.” It later emerged that producers had assessed the rapper as “high risk” and yet decided to broadcast his set live.

Even as he embarked on his rant, which BBC chair Samir Shah later acknowledged consisted of “unconscionable antisemitic views,” no one at the broadcaster thought to cut the Glastonbury feed. Shah apologized for the oversight, and the BBC’s director of music, Lorna Clarke, briefly “stepped back” from her duties, although it appears little other action was taken (she has long since returned to her post).

Then, last month, it was revealed that the BBC had reached an out-of-court settlement with one of its top factual producers, Lucie Kon, after she brought a legal claim alleging antisemitic discrimination. Kon, an Emmy and Oscar winner who exec produced “Mr Nobody Against Putin,” had worked for the corporation for 25 years but said that after Oct. 7, when Hamas murdered 1,200 people in Israel and kidnapped 250 more, the atmosphere toward her changed.

The BBC rejected those claims but agreed to pay Kon £400,000 ($520,000) to settle out of court. For health reasons, Kon accepted. By comparison, the average award handed down by courts for race discrimination in the U.K. is £29,532, according to the most recent statistics.

At the same time, the BBC’s reporting on Israel has been an ongoing source of contention. There was the Gaza documentary which failed to tell viewers the narrator was the son of a senior Hamas official, the report speculating Israel had bombed a hospital in Gaza which had actually been hit by a Hamas rocket misfiring and the news story in which an anchor misrepresented a Reuters story, saying the IDF was “targeting … medical teams as well as Arabic speakers” when in fact the medical teams and Arabic speakers were part of the IDF, there to assess patients on the ground.

A leaked internal report last year — the same one that led to BBC boss Tim Davie resigning when it revealed the BBC had doctored one of President Trump’s speeches — noted that BBC Arabic, a part of the corporation’s World Service, had made 215 corrections and clarifications in its reporting of the Israel-Gaza war since 2023, amounting to two a week. At the time, a BBC spokesperson told Variety: “BBC News Arabic strives for the highest standards of journalism across its services.”

(Incidentally, the BBC World Service currently operates in 45 languages, including Arabic, Amharic, English, Hausa, Kirundi, Marathi, Tigrinya, Ukrainian, Urdu and Yoruba. It does not include Hebrew.)

So how did the BBC find itself embroiled in yet another crisis?

Part of the problem stems from the fact that the corporation effectively marks its own homework. While British newspapers are regulated by an independent body, IPSO, the BBC operates the Executive Complaints Unit to investigate grievances about itself.

But there is also a sense that the BBC, even under its new director general Matt Brittin, is not interested in engaging seriously with the issue. Each time there is a public blunder, the BBC will roll out the same playbook: issue a cut-and-paste apology (usually with reluctance), defend its reporting and make a gesture to suggest it has learned a lesson. But the sheer frequency of incidents — only a handful of which even spin out into the public realm — suggests nothing is being learned.

Earlier this month, the corporation’s deputy director-general, Rhodri Talfan Davies, was asked during an on-the-record Q&A session with journalists whether he would support an internal inquiry into antisemitism at the BBC. His response was to deny there was a “deep-rooted issue” or any “institutional discrimination” at the broadcaster. Notably, he didn’t answer the second part of the journalist’s question, namely, if Talfan Davies didn’t think there was antisemitism at the BBC, “Why do you think many of your Jewish employees think there is?”

Even the corporation’s checkbox response to Lord Mann’s announcement on Thursday gives the impression, whether intended or not, that the threat of an investigation into its internal conduct is of little consequence. When approached for comment, a BBC publicist told Variety by email, “We’d also like to direct you to the below statement, that we’ve previously issued,” before copy-and-pasting it underneath.

In his speech announcing the investigation, Lord Mann said he is “not interested in targeting individuals. That would entirely miss the point. I am targeting the institution.” The biggest clue as to the depth of the BBC’s antisemitism problem will be whether the institution even cares.

#646. A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics

A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide new insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

There is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a new technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors

Previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

Unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

The UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

If cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

"The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," said Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as new physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted."

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data

To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an important independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

The new approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

To demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the new method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe

The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

One known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter

The challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

This kind of independent verification will become increasingly important as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement."

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

Although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most important unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

One possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely new way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those currently understood.

For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

Materials provided by University of California - San Diego. Original written by Michelle Franklin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#644. Matt Damon Narrates Ford Racing’s ‘Go Like Hell’ Thanksgiving Day Ad Directed by Zack Snyder

Ford Racing tapped Matt Damon, star of “Ford v Ferrari,” to introduce the all-new Ford GT41 Hypercar in a new ad directed by filmmaker Zack Snyder.

The ad is slated to air during CBS’s broadcast of the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears Thanksgiving Day NFL game, which starts at 1 p.m. ET. The 90-second spot centers on the GT41 Hypercar and the U.S. automaker’s return to the top class of the FIA World Endurance Championship and Le Mans in 2027 — and evoking Damon’s turn as a driver in “Ford v Ferrari.” The ad was produced by Artists Equity, the studio led by Damon and Ben Affleck. (Watch the full spot below.) Related Stories 'Ramayana' VFX House DNEG Partners With Meta on 3D Movies for VR Glasses, Including 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' (EXCLUSIVE) Meta Launches 150-Plus 3D Movies to Rent and Buy on Quest VR Headsets, With Thousands More Coming in 2027

“What does it mean to be American?” Damon says in the ad. “Well, many things to many people. To us, it’s not just where we hang our hat. It’s downright relentless grit.” The spot ends with Damon praising Ford Racing fans: “More than part of the team, you’re our fuel. Why we persevere. Every mile feeds the next. Because that’s what it means to be American. That we always — without fail — go like hell.”

The spot chronicles the journey of Ford’s GT41 Hypercar from the U.S. to the legendary Circuit de la Sarthe in Le Mans, France, ahead of its competitive debut in 2027. The film was shot in and around Los Angeles, symbolizing “Ford Racing’s return to the scene of some of its greatest motorsport triumphs,” according to the car company. It also features connections to “Ford v Ferrari”: For example, the airplane hangar used to load the GT41’s shipping container is the same one used for the Ford GT40 race workshop in the movie.

Damon, who serves as chief content officer of Artists Equity, portrayed Ford driver Carroll Shelby in 2019’s “Ford v Ferrari.”

“Telling the story of Le Mans ‘66 [in ‘Ford v Ferrari’] was one of the highlights of my career, so getting to lend my voice to the next chapter felt very full circle,” Damon said in a statement. “Revisiting this one with Ford and Zack, as they take on the world’s toughest racing all over again, was a real privilege.”

Snyder, known for films including “300,” “Watchmen” and “Justice League,” commented: “The amazing part about getting a chance to work on this ‘Go Like Hell’ spot for Ford Racing was the chance to mix the nostalgia of the ’66 GT40 with this modern hypercar and its incredible engineering as well as this narrative that follows the transporting of the car across America.”

The ad coincides with Thursday’s official public unveiling of the Ford GT41 at Detroit’s Ford Field. The new vehicle takes its name from the Ford GT40, which secured four consecutive overall victories at Le Mans between 1966 and 1969. Like its predecessor, the GT41’s name reflects its dimensions, standing 41 inches from the ground to the air intake.

The Ford GT41 will make its competitive debut in the 2027 FIA World Endurance Championship, with the season opening in Qatar in March before the team heads to Le Mans in June.

#643. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

"I'd lost the plot," says the disgraced ex-BBC newsreader in a teaser for 'Huw Edwards - Guilty.'

“From trusted national figure to registered sex offender,” says a voiceover in a new documentary for Channel 4, Huw Edwards – Guilty.

The disgraced former BBC anchor is speaking publicly for the first time since the scandal that rocked Britain, letting cameras into his home over the course of a year. The film follows Edwards as he navigates his existence in the wake of grooming allegations and his 2024 conviction for making indecent images of children.

The journalist becomes the subject in a teaser released by Channel 4 on Thursday, as Edwards becomes visibly fraught while questioned. “You want me to analyze what I was doing? The ex-newscaster, who hosted the BBC’s flagship News at Ten program and led landmark coverage for the corporation — including the death of Queen Elizabeth II and the London 2012 Olympics — was arrested in November 2023 and charged the following July after he was found to have 41 indecent images of children sent to him by another man, a convicted pedophile, on WhatsApp. Seven of the photos were category A images, the most severe classification, two of which showed a child between seven and nine. He was handed a six-month sentence, suspended for two years.

Following several attempts to ingratiate himself back into public life, Channel 4 says Edwards is forced to confront his loss of fame, declining health, fractured relationships, and his crimes in the documentary.

It comes a few months down the line from 5’s dramatized program on the scandal, with Wuthering Heights star Martin Clunes taking on the titular role in Power: The Downfall of Huw Edwards.

The Welshman angrily bashed the series at the time, condemning the producers for making “no attempt to check with me the truth of any aspect of their narrative before going ahead with the production.” A rep for 5 maintained that all allegations made were put to the ex-broadcaster six weeks before the show’s premiere.

Channel 4’s Huw Edwards – Guilty will air on Dec. 1.

“This was an important film to make,” says director Patrick Forbes. “It’s rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary issues — whether it’s celebrity culture or the power of the media — as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment.”

Huw Edwards – Guilty was commissioned by Sacha Mirzoeff, senior commissioning editor at Channel 4 and produced by Oxford Films. It is directed by Patrick Forbes. The producer is Stephanie Collins. The EPs are Vanessa Tuson and Nick Kent.

#641. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising new direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," says Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether."

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures."

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

Materials provided by Utrecht University, Faculty of Science. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#638. Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

A new project and exhibition, "The Night Watch Lives," lifts the veil on the hidden world of microbes covering one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.

Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius."

In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.

Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.

The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?

The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention."

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch."

Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.

These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.

At the exhibition's opening on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the coming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.

That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us."

People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," says van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013.  How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery."

The samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again."

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.

As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch.'"

The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.

And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project."

The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

#637. More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but new research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he said.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath new deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A New Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

This agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

The research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle."

Materials provided by University of Wollongong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#636. Jessy Moussallem’s ‘Faux Bijoux,’ Laila Abbas’ ‘America Is Behind the Door’ Take Top Prizes at Marrakech’s Atlas Workshops

Jessy Moussallem’s “Faux Bijoux” and Laila Abbas’ “America Is Behind the Door” claimed the top post-production and development prizes, respectively, at this year’s Atlas Workshops, the industry strand running Nov. 22 – 26 as part of the Marrakech Film Festival.

The winner of a post-production grant in the amount of €30,000 ($33,000), Moussallem’s debut feature is an expansion of the short film of the same name, which screened at Sundance and Clermont-Ferrand. It follows the members of a family who are caught up in debts and schemes that drag them into a vicious cycle and test their unity. Related Stories Jesse Eisenberg and Julianne Moore on ‘The Debut,’ Testing AI to ‘Make Sure It’s Bad’ and Hoping ‘Now You See Me 4’ Gets Made Is ‘I Play Rocky’ Original or Adapted? Stallone’s ‘Rocky’ Origin Story Faces a ‘Barbie’-Style Oscar Dilemma (EXCLUSIVE)

With principal photography underway, the Lebanese filmmaker couldn’t attend the Atlas Workshops. In a director’s statement, she wrote: “‘Faux Bijoux’ was born from a question rooted in my family and in Lebanon: Why is truth sometimes too difficult to speak? Behind our obsession with appearances lies a struggle for dignity, and a desire to protect those we love.” She added: “The film explores how love survives unspoken truths, and how lying can become its only possible language.”

The post-production jury of festival programmer and distributor Eddie Bertozzi (Be Water Film), filmmaker Mohamed Kordofani (“Goodbye Julia”) and artistic director Kristy Matheson (BFI Festivals) awarded the second prize of €10,000 ($11,000) to two films: “Hamlet From the Slums,” by Ahmed Fawzi-Saleh, and “Occupational Hazards,” by Bassel Ghandour.

Following his 2018 Rotterdam premiere “Poisonous Roses,” Egyptian filmmaker Fawzi-Saleh’s sophomore feature follows Ahmed, a restless and stifled young man who lives under the strict rule of his widower father, the self-proclaimed “King of the Junkyard.” When a revelation sets off a chain of events no one can control, Ahmed is drawn into a search for the truth that will cost him everything.

Jordanian writer, director and producer Ghandour wrote and produced the Academy Award-nominated film “Theeb.” His directorial debut, “The Alleys,” premiered at Locarno’s Piazza Grande. Set in Jerusalem, “Occupational Hazards” follows a Palestinian family that fights to keep their home from crumbling, both literally and figuratively, as their struggle against the system takes on wild and unorthodox forms.

The third prize, in the amount of €10,000 ($11,000), went to “My Father Killed Bourguiba,” by Fatma Riahi. The latest from the Tunisian director, whose debut, “A Haunted Past,” premiered at IDFA in 2018, is a deeply personal journey into the story of the filmmaker’s father, who was part of a failed coup attempt against Tunisia’s first president, Habib Bourguiba.

Development jurors Nadim Cheikhrouha (Mime Films), Marie-Ange Luciani (Les Films de Pierre) and Linda Mutawi (Fikra) awarded the top prize of €25,000 ($27,400) to the Palestinian filmmaker Abbas, whose debut “Thank You for Banking With Us!” premiered at the BFI London Film Festival in 2024.

Her sophomore feature follows an exhausted Palestinian mother who faces a series of impossible confrontations over the course of the 10 days before her U.S. citizenship interview. The closer that fateful day comes, the less she can separate suburban life from a genocide enabled by the country of which she is about to become.

“I am interested in what politics does to human behavior: how it changes the way people parent, argue, joke, choose silence, or decide to speak,” Abbas wrote in a director’s statement. “As a Palestinian filmmaker, I am drawn to moments when absurdity and grief occupy the same space, because that is where life feels most truthful to me.

“At a moment when Palestine feels almost impossible to speak about outside the immediacy of catastrophe, I choose to tell this story from a distance. Setting the film in the United States gives me a wider lens through which to look back at Palestine — to hold grief and anger without being consumed by them, and to examine political and human contradictions with greater clarity,” she continued. “The film engages with the role of the United States in sustaining the destruction in Palestine, while exposing the contradiction between the country’s founding promise as a place for immigrants and the realities many immigrants encounter now.”

The development jury awarded its second prize of €10,000 ($11,000) to “Waltz of the Savages,” by Yasmine Benkiran, whose first feature, “Queens,” premiered at the Venice Film Festival. The Moroccan-born filmmaker’s latest is set in the 1950s in an Arab country under French colonial rule, where the most lavish party in the nation’s history is about to be staged, while outside, rebellion brews.

The third prize of €10,000 ($11,000) went to “Eko Gongon,” by Cabo Verde’s Carlos Yuri Ceuninck, whose last documentary, “Omi Nobu,” won the top prize at Burkina Faso’s FESPACO film festival. The film takes place in a fishing village threatened by globalization, where the Gongon — a rare endemic seabird and a phantasmagoric, shapeshifting figure from oral tradition — haunts the archipelago’s imagination.

The fourth prize of €5,000 ($5,500) went to “Safara,” a feature debut by Senegalese filmmaker Awa Moctar Gueye, which follows the trials of a tomboyish teenager on the suffocating streets of Safara, a neighborhood whose name means “hell.” The fifth prize of €5,000 ($5,500) went to “Chronicles of an Unannounced Death,” by Syrian German writer, director and producer Dyaa Naim. It follows a Syrian undertaker living in Germany whose life and past are turned upside down when he learns his recently deceased father wanted to be buried in Damascus.

Lastly, the Atlas Close-Ups jury, which was comprised of producer Amine Benjelloun (Ali n’ Productions) and programmer Delly Shirazi (Intl. Film Festival Rotterdam), gave a prize of €5,000 ($5,500) to “The Cemetery’s Bird,” by writer-director Madane El Ghazouani, awarding it for its “boldness, a big heart and something new as a cinematic proposal for Morocco’s national cinema.” El Ghazouani’s first feature, “Bad Weather,” won four prizes at the Marrakech Film Festival in 2025.

Since their inception in 2018, the Atlas Workshops have supported 242 projects — including 111 Moroccan films — with 42 of those having been selected by Cannes, Venice or Berlin. Nearly half the films in this year’s main competition in Marrakech are alumni of the program, including Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Cannes Camera d’Or winner “Ben’Imana” and Rafiki Fariala’s Un Certain Regard prizewinner “Congo Boy.”

At Thursday’s ceremony, Marrakech festival director and Atlas Workshops founder Rémi Bonhomme celebrated the “rich program” at this year’s edition, underscoring how the participants continue to make the event “a very vibrant place for Arab and African cinema.”

“The Atlas Workshops is a spirit. It’s a spirit that has been the same since the very first edition in 2018,” Bonhomme said. “How to define the spirit of the Workshops? I think it has a lot to do with the conviction to place the filmmaker and the creative process at the heart of everything we do. We really support the vision. We really accompany them and support them in making the boldest film as possible.

“We live in a time when we need, more than ever, free and daring cinematic voices. We really need voices that can challenge dominant narratives,” Bonhomme added. “We need voices that can really change our perspective of the world, and I truly think that’s what we do here at the Atlas Workshops, edition after edition.”

The Marrakech Film Festival runs through Nov. 28.
